claim: DNA viruses in the family Poxviridae encode poxin enzymes that degrade the immune second messenger 2′3′-cGAMP to inhibit cGAS-STING immunity in mammalian cells.
source: DNA viruses in the family Poxviridae encode poxin enzymes that degrade the immune second messenger 2′3′-cGAMP to inhibit cGAS-STING immunity in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references to previous work (Eaglesham et al., 2019) and experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The closest homologs of poxin exist in the genomes of insect viruses.
source: The closest homologs of poxin exist in the genomes of insect viruses suggesting a key mechanism of cGAS-STING evasion may have evolved outside of mammalian biology.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis (PSI-BLAST searches) and phylogenetic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A broad family of 369 poxins is encoded in diverse viral and animal genomes.
source: Here we use a biochemical and structural approach to discover a broad family of 369 poxins encoded in diverse viral and animal genomes and define a prominent role for 2′3′-cGAMP cleavage in metazoan host-pathogen conflict.
evidence: This is supported by PSI-BLAST searches described in the Materials and methods section and the identification of sequences in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Structures of insect poxins reveal unexpected homology to flavivirus proteases.
source: Structures of insect poxins reveal unexpected homology to flavivirus proteases and enable identification of functional self-cleaving poxins in RNA-virus polyproteins.
evidence: This is supported by X-ray crystal structures and DALI structural homology analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: Functional self-cleaving poxins exist in RNA-virus polyproteins.
source: Structures of insect poxins reveal unexpected homology to flavivirus proteases and enable identification of functional self-cleaving poxins in RNA-virus polyproteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical assays showing both nuclease and protease activity in amarillovirus poxins (Figure 5).

claim: A family of cGAS-STING evasion enzymes evolved from viral proteases through gain of secondary nuclease activity.
source: Our data suggest widespread 2′3′-cGAMP signaling in insect antiviral immunity and explain how a family of cGAS-STING evasion enzymes evolved from viral proteases through gain of secondary nuclease activity.
evidence: This is supported by structural homology to viral proteases, identification of vestigial protease active sites, and functional characterization of dual-activity enzymes.

claim: Poxin acquisition by poxviruses demonstrates the importance of environmental connections in shaping evolution of mammalian pathogens.
source: Poxin acquisition by poxviruses demonstrates the importance of environmental connections in shaping evolution of mammalian pathogens.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of poxins showing presence in insect viruses and hosts before acquisition by mammalian poxviruses.

claim: The cGAS-STING pathway is a major sensor of pathogen infection in mammalian cells.
source: The cGAS-STING pathway is a major sensor of pathogen infection in mammalian cells where it functions to detect mislocalized cytosolic DNA exposed during infection (Ablasser and Chen, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: cGAS binds directly to cytosolic DNA and becomes activated to synthesize 2′3′-cGAMP.
source: The enzyme cyclic GMP–AMP synthase (cGAS) binds directly to cytosolic DNA, and becomes activated to synthesize the nucleotide second messenger 2′–5′/3′–5′ cyclic GMP–AMP (2′3′-cGAMP) (Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: 2′3′-cGAMP is recognized by the receptor STING, which oligomerizes and recruits downstream signaling adapters to drive induction of type I interferon and NF-κB signaling.
source: 2′3′-cGAMP is then recognized by the receptor Stimulator of Interferon Genes (STING), which oligomerizes and recruits downstream signaling adapters to drive induction of type I interferon and NF-κB signaling (Figure 1A; Ablasser et al., 2013; Diner et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Poxin enzymes inhibit cGAS-STING signaling by degrading 2′3′-cGAMP and blocking activation of STING.
source: Poxin enzymes inhibit cGAS-STING signaling by degrading 2′3′-cGAMP and blocking activation of STING.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A, supported by previous work (Eaglesham et al., 2019).

claim: Poxins can be divided into four major groups based on their genomic origins.
source: Poxins can be divided into groups, including enzymes from mammalian and insect poxviruses (Group 1), parasitoid wasps and alphabaculoviruses (Group 2), moths and butterflies (Lepidoptera) (Group 3), and cypoviruses, betabaculoviruses, and betaentomopoxviruses (Group 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phylogenetic analysis and biochemical characterization shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Poxin 2′3′-cGAMP nuclease activity is conserved within each group.
source: Poxin 2′3′-cGAMP nuclease activity is conserved within each group.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TLC assays showing 2′3′-cGAMP degradation by representatives from all groups in Figure 1B.

claim: Poxviruses replicate exclusively in the cytosol.
source: Poxviruses are large DNA viruses which replicate exclusively in the cytosol (Moss, 2013), and encode poxvirus immune nucleases (poxins) to degrade 2′3′-cGAMP and prevent STING activation (Figure 1A; Eaglesham et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Vaccinia virus poxin is sufficient to antagonize cGAS-STING signaling in cells and is necessary for effective viral replication in vivo.
source: Vaccinia virus (VACV) poxin (encoded by the gene B2R) is sufficient to antagonize cGAS-STING signaling in cells and is necessary for effective viral replication in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Eaglesham et al., 2019).

claim: VACV poxin catalysis proceeds through a metal-independent mechanism, contorting 2′3′-cGAMP into a conformation that activates the 2′ hydroxyl for in-line cleavage of the 3′–5′ bond.
source: Crystal structures of VACV poxin in the pre- and post-reactive states revealed that catalysis proceeds through a metal-independent mechanism, contorting 2′3′-cGAMP into a conformation that activates the 2′ hydroxyl for in-line cleavage of the 3′–5′ bond (Eaglesham et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural work.

claim: Poxviruses have a well-documented ability to acquire genes horizontally, especially from their hosts.
source: Poxviruses have a well-documented ability to acquire genes horizontally, especially from their hosts (Hughes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The closest homologs of VACV poxin belong to baculoviruses and Lepidoptera.
source: The closest homologs of VACV poxin belong not to mammals or other mammalian viruses, but to baculoviruses, and Lepidoptera (moths and butterflies) which serve as exclusive hosts of baculoviruses (Eaglesham et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis and citation to previous work.

claim: Baculovirus and lepidopteran poxin homologs share <25% identity with VACV poxin.
source: While baculovirus and lepidopteran poxin homologs share <25% identity with VACV poxin, they are functional nucleases and retain 2′3′-cGAMP-specific cleavage activity (Eaglesham et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and biochemical characterization.

claim: Baculovirus and lepidopteran poxin homologs are functional nucleases and retain 2′3′-cGAMP-specific cleavage activity.
source: While baculovirus and lepidopteran poxin homologs share <25% identity with VACV poxin, they are functional nucleases and retain 2′3′-cGAMP-specific cleavage activity (Eaglesham et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays and citation to previous work.

claim: PSI-BLAST searches identified an initial combined total of 351 unique poxin-like sequences.
source: To define poxin diversity and phylogenetic distribution, we used both the VACV poxin and lepidopteran Trichoplusia ni poxin sequences to seed position-specific iterative BLAST (PSI-BLAST) searches, identifying an initial combined total of 351 unique poxin-like sequences.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis described in the Materials and methods.

claim: Poxin homologs can be classified into four major enzyme groups with <25% identity to one another.
source: Poxin homologs can be classified into four major enzyme groups with <25% identity to one another and which share seven different phylogenetic origins (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and phylogenetic trees shown in the figures.

claim: 33 diverse poxin representatives were cloned and directly tested for 2′3′-cGAMP nuclease activity.
source: We cloned 33 diverse representatives and directly tested recombinant protein for 2′3′-cGAMP nuclease activity using thin-layer chromatography (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Poxin homologs from all groups efficiently degraded 2′3′-cGAMP.
source: Poxin homologs from all groups efficiently degraded 2′3′-cGAMP (Figure 1B), demonstrating nuclease activity is a conserved function of this protein family regardless of the sequence origin or genomic context.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TLC assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Nuclease activity is a conserved function of the poxin protein family regardless of sequence origin or genomic context.
source: Poxin homologs from all groups efficiently degraded 2′3′-cGAMP (Figure 1B), demonstrating nuclease activity is a conserved function of this protein family regardless of the sequence origin or genomic context.
evidence: This is inferred from the biochemical data showing activity across all tested groups.

claim: Group 2 poxins primarily contain enzymes encoded in alphabaculovirus genomes.
source: Group two primarily contains poxins encoded in alphabaculovirus genomes.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and sequence classification.

claim: Two poxin sequences identified in parasitoid wasp genomes cluster alongside alphabaculovirus enzymes.
source: However, two sequences identified in the genomes of parasitoid wasps (Microplitis demolitor and Glypta fumiferanae) cluster alongside these viral enzymes.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Parasitoid wasps parasitize caterpillars, laying their eggs inside them and co-injecting domesticated bracoviruses which modulate caterpillar immunity.
source: These wasps parasitize caterpillars, laying their eggs inside them and co-injecting domesticated bracoviruses which modulate caterpillar immunity to favor egg maturation (Béliveau et al., 2015; Burke et al., 2018; Strand and Burke, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Lepidopteran poxin enzymes have been shown to be highly upregulated after infection with various pathogens.
source: Lepidopteran poxin enzymes cluster within Group 3, and have been shown to be highly upregulated after infection with various pathogens, including alphabaculoviruses and bacteria, providing evidence for a role in immunity or immune regulation (Shrestha et al., 2019; Woon Shin et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous transcriptional studies.

claim: Group 4 is formed by poxin proteins from the genomes of betabaculoviruses, cypoviruses, and betaentomopoxviruses.
source: Group four is formed by poxin proteins from the genomes of several additional lepidopteran viruses: betabaculoviruses (also called granuloviruses), cypoviruses (double-stranded RNA viruses in the family Reoviridae), and betaentomopoxviruses (Figure 1B; Silva et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic classification shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The evolutionary distance between DNA and RNA viral families suggests related poxin genes may have been transferred between viruses within coinfected cells.
source: The vast evolutionary distance between these DNA and RNA viral families suggests related poxin genes may have been transferred between viruses within coinfected cells (Silva et al., 2020; Thézé et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis and supported by citations.

claim: The enormous diversity of poxin enzymes in insect pathogens and moth and butterfly genomes confirms a broad role for 2′3′-cGAMP degradation.
source: Notably, the enormous diversity of poxin enzymes in insect pathogens and moth and butterfly genomes confirms a broad role for 2′3′-cGAMP degradation, and strongly suggests these genomes served as a source for emergence of poxins in mammalian poxviruses.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution and biochemical activity data.

claim: Insect genomes strongly suggest they served as a source for emergence of poxins in mammalian poxviruses.
source: Notably, the enormous diversity of poxin enzymes in insect pathogens and moth and butterfly genomes confirms a broad role for 2′3′-cGAMP degradation, and strongly suggests these genomes served as a source for emergence of poxins in mammalian poxviruses.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis showing greater diversity in insect-associated poxins.

claim: Crystal structures were determined for AcNPV poxin, T. ni poxin, D. plexippus poxin, and PrGV poxin in complex with 2′3′-cGAMP.
source: To enable comparative analysis with VACV poxin (Group 1), we next determined a series of structures of representative enzymes from Groups 2–4 in complex with 2′3′-cGAMP. New poxin structures include the alphabaculovirus Autographa californica nucleopolyhedrovirus (AcNPV) poxin from Group 2, lepidopteran host poxins from the moth Trichoplusia ni and the monarch butterfly Danaus plexippus in Group 3, and the betabaculovirus Pieris rapae granulovirus (PrGV) poxin from Group 4 (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by X-ray crystallography data presented in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Poxin structures from each group reveal a shared core fold and head-to-tail dimeric architecture.
source: In spite of dramatic sequence divergence, poxin structures from each group reveal a shared core fold and head-to-tail dimeric architecture confirming poxins as a single enzyme family (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural comparison shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Despite differences in active-site residues, 2′3′-cGAMP is contorted within each structure into a similar strained conformation.
source: Despite differences in active-site residues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C), 2′3′-cGAMP is contorted within each structure into a similar strained conformation, confirming that poxins operate by the same core metal-independent mechanism established for VACV poxin.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural comparison shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Poxins operate by the same core metal-independent mechanism established for VACV poxin.
source: Despite differences in active-site residues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C), 2′3′-cGAMP is contorted within each structure into a similar strained conformation, confirming that poxins operate by the same core metal-independent mechanism established for VACV poxin.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison and supported by previous mechanistic studies.

claim: VACV and AcNPV poxin share a conserved active-site triad of histidine, tyrosine, and lysine residues.
source: Unlike the catalytic triad of histidine, tyrosine, and lysine residues essential for VACV and AcNPV poxin cleavage activity (Figure 2B,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C), the active sites of T. ni poxin and PrGV poxin are divergent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural analysis and mutagenesis shown in Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: T. ni and PrGV poxin enzymes contain altered active-site triads composed of two histidines and an arginine or lysine residue.
source: The T. ni and PrGV poxin enzymes share the conserved active-site histidine but lack a tyrosine residue entirely (Figure 2D,E). Instead, both proteins contain a second histidine residue adjacent to the first, which forms a contact with the 2′ hydroxyl or 3′ phosphate of the cleaved 2′3′-cGAMP molecule (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural analysis shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The second histidine residue in T. ni poxin is essential for activity.
source: In the case of T. ni poxin, mutagenesis analysis demonstrates this second histidine residue is essential for activity, suggesting this residue functions as a general base to deprotonate and activate the 2′ hydroxyl nucleophile for in-line cleavage of the 3′–5′ bond (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: VACV and AcNPV poxin exhibit similar kinetics with KM values of 0.83 µM and 2.43 µM respectively.
source: Interestingly, mammalian and insect viral poxins from VACV and AcNPV exhibit similar kinetics, with a KM of 0.83 µM and 2.43 µM respectively, while the T. ni host poxin protein has a KM two orders of magnitude higher at 342.1 µM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by enzyme kinetics measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: T. ni host poxin has a KM two orders of magnitude higher at 342.1 µM compared to viral poxins.
source: Interestingly, mammalian and insect viral poxins from VACV and AcNPV exhibit similar kinetics, with a KM of 0.83 µM and 2.43 µM respectively, while the T. ni host poxin protein has a KM two orders of magnitude higher at 342.1 µM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by enzyme kinetics measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: T. ni poxin has a much higher rate constant of 2254 min−1 compared to VACV and AcNPV poxin (93.4 min−1 and 346 min−1, respectively).
source: However, the host T. ni poxin has a much higher rate constant of 2254 min−1 compared to VACV and AcNPV poxin (93.4 min−1 and 346 min−1, respectively).
evidence: This is demonstrated by enzyme kinetics measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inactive VACV and AcNPV poxin exhibited a KD of 0.58 µM and 0.81 µM respectively.
source: Consistent with our enzyme kinetics results, inactive VACV and AcNPV poxin exhibited a KD of 0.58 µM and 0.81 µM respectively, within a similar range as the respective KM values of wild-type enzymes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by gel shift assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E–H.

claim: The KD of catalytic site mutant T. ni poxin is higher than 20 µM.
source: In contrast, we could not measure the KD of the catalytic site mutant T. ni poxin, indicating it is higher than 20 µM, again consistent with the high KM value for wildtype T. ni poxin.
evidence: This is demonstrated by gel shift assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Viral poxins are adapted to depletion of 2′3′-cGAMP to low levels, while host poxin is adapted for regulation and efficient clearance of 2′3′-cGAMP after accumulation to higher concentrations.
source: Although animal studies will be required to understand the biological role of diverse poxins, our biochemical analysis is consistent with a model where viral poxins are adapted to depletion of 2′3′-cGAMP to low levels, while the host poxin is adapted for regulation and efficient clearance of 2′3′-cGAMP after accumulation to higher concentrations.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic differences observed between viral and host poxins.

claim: Host poxin genes are strongly upregulated during baculovirus infection in a second wave of transcription occurring after initial immune induction.
source: Further supporting these results, studies of the lepidopteran transcriptional response to baculovirus infection show that host poxin genes are strongly upregulated during infection in a second wave of transcription occurring after initial immune induction (Shrestha et al., 2019; Woon Shin et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to transcriptional studies.

claim: The N-terminal domain of VACV poxin exhibits weak homology to chymotrypsin-like serine proteases.
source: Although poxin functions as a 2′3′-cGAMP-specific nuclease, previous analysis of VACV poxin demonstrated that no structural homology exists with other nuclease or phosphodiesterase enzymes (Eaglesham et al., 2019). Instead, the N-terminal domain of VACV poxin exhibits weak homology to chymotrypsin-like serine proteases (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DALI structural homology analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: T. ni poxin structure demonstrates strong homology with proteases derived from (+)ssRNA viruses.
source: Analysis of the host T. ni poxin structure confirms a relationship with protease enzymes and demonstrates strong homology with proteases derived from (+)ssRNA viruses (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DALI structural homology analysis shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The N-terminal domain of T. ni poxin demonstrates near complete conservation of a dual Greek key β-barrel fold common to serine protease enzymes.
source: Unlike the degenerated domain in VACV poxin, comparison of the N-terminal domain of T. ni poxin with the yellow fever virus protease demonstrates near complete conservation of a dual Greek key β-barrel fold common to serine protease enzymes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural comparison shown in Figure 3C.

claim: T. ni poxin likely retains extensive ancestral protease homology due to the slow evolutionary rate of insect host genomes compared to viral genes.
source: Like a molecular fossil, T. ni poxin likely retains extensive ancestral protease homology due to the slow evolutionary rate of insect host genomes compared to the rapid replication and divergence of viral genes (Duffy et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from structural conservation and supported by citation on evolutionary rates.

claim: All poxins share a C-terminal domain required for dimerization and formation of the nuclease active site.
source: In addition to the N-terminal protease domain, all poxins share a C-terminal domain required for dimerization and formation of the nuclease active site. Accordingly, this domain is highly conserved with no degeneration occurring between VACV and T. ni poxin (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural comparison shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A nuclease dedicated to 2′3′-cGAMP degradation evolved through dimerization and divergence of an ancient viral protease.
source: Together these results reveal unexpectedly close homology between poxin and protease enzymes and suggest a nuclease dedicated to 2′3′-cGAMP degradation evolved through dimerization and divergence of an ancient viral protease.
evidence: This is inferred from structural homology analysis and evolutionary relationships.

claim: (+)ssRNA viruses typically encode gene products as a polyprotein that must be proteolytically cleaved to release individual mature peptides.
source: (+)ssRNA viruses typically encode gene products as a polyprotein that must be proteolytically cleaved to release individual mature peptides (Lei and Hilgenfeld, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: (+)ssRNA viruses often possess accessory proteases which excise themselves from the polyprotein and serve alternative structural or immune antagonist roles.
source: Additionally, (+)ssRNA viruses often possess accessory proteases which excise themselves from the polyprotein and serve alternative structural or immune antagonist roles (Lei and Hilgenfeld, 2017; Mann and Sanfaçon, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: A nearly identical pocket is conserved on the surface of the T. ni poxin protease-like domain, in which the poxin C-terminus is coordinated by histidine and aspartic acid residues.
source: A nearly identical pocket is conserved on the surface of the T. ni poxin protease-like domain, in which the poxin C-terminus is also coordinated by histidine and aspartic acid residues (Figure 4B,D,G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural analysis shown in Figure 4B,D,G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The final five residues in the C-terminal peptide in lepidopteran poxin proteins are highly conserved.
source: The final five residues in the C-terminal peptide in lepidopteran poxin proteins are highly conserved (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and bind within the protease-domain pocket through hydrophobic interactions where each residue resides within a pocket of corresponding size and shape.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural analysis and sequence alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Lepidopteran poxins retain a protease-like mechanism for recognition and positioning of the C-terminus within a vestigial protease active site.
source: Authentic proteases recognize their substrates through similar sidechain-specific interactions within pockets adjacent to the active site, demonstrating that lepidopteran poxins retain a protease-like mechanism for recognition and positioning of the C-terminus within a vestigial protease active site (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C; Hedstrom, 2002).
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison with authentic proteases and supported by citation.

claim: Viral poxins from AcNPV and VACV reveal greater degeneration in the protease domain and protease active-site pocket resulting in loss of C-terminal coordination.
source: Comparison of lepidopteran poxins with viral poxins from AcNPV and VACV reveals greater degeneration in the protease domain and protease active-site pocket in viral enzymes that results in loss of C-terminal coordination (Figure 3A, Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural comparison shown in Figure 4E–G.

claim: The protease active-site pocket is entirely distinct from the poxin nuclease active site, which forms at the dimer interface between poxin monomers.
source: Notably, the protease active-site pocket is entirely distinct from the poxin nuclease active site, which forms at the dimer interface between poxin monomers (Figure 2A, Figure 4B,G), explaining how 2′3′-cGAMP nuclease activity could evolve independently within an ancestral self-cleaving accessory protease.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 4B,G.

claim: Later expression of poxins from a discrete open reading frame likely released selective pressure for maintenance of self-cleavage activity and resulted in protease-domain degeneration.
source: Later expression of poxins from a discrete open reading frame in insect hosts or other viruses likely released selective pressure for maintenance of self-cleavage activity and resulted in protease-domain degeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of protease domain degeneration observed in different poxin groups.

claim: Eight (+)ssRNA flavivirus-like viruses encode divergent poxin-like regions within large polyproteins.
source: Re-examination of our initial PSI-BLAST results (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) revealed additional short (92–195 amino acids), divergent poxin-like regions within large 5,901–8572 amino acid long polyproteins of eight (+)ssRNA flavivirus-like viruses that are unclassified members of the order Amarillovirales (Koonin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis described in the text.

claim: These (+)ssRNA viral genomes were originally characterized through RNA sequencing of diverse insects and likely represent insect-specific viruses.
source: These genomes were originally characterized through RNA sequencing of diverse insects and likely represent insect-specific viruses (Kobayashi et al., 2013; Remnant et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2016; Teixeira et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous sequencing studies.

claim: The (+)ssRNA viral poxin sequences are highly divergent, sharing between 10–25% identity with one another.
source: The (+)ssRNA viral poxin sequences are highly divergent, sharing between 10–25% identity with one another, and occur in variable genome positions including at the extreme N-terminus and up to 1000 amino acids inside the predicted viral polyprotein (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Alignment of the (+)ssRNA viral poxin sequences reveals conservation of putative protease catalytic residues (histidine, aspartate, and serine).
source: Alignment of the (+)ssRNA viral poxin sequences reveals conservation of putative protease catalytic residues (histidine, aspartate, and serine) (Figure 5B), with the catalytic serine residing in an SGTP motif that is consistent with the vestigial AGTP motif conserved in the lepidopteran poxin protease active site (Figure 5B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence alignment shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Amarillovirus poxin proteins from Macrosiphum euphorbiae virus 1, Gamboa mosquito virus, and XCV retain 2′3′-cGAMP nuclease activity.
source: Activity analysis demonstrates that (+)ssRNA viral poxins from Macrosiphum euphorbiae virus 1, Gamboa mosquito virus, and Xingshan cricket virus (XCV) efficiently catalyze 2′3′-cGAMP degradation verifying these proteins as functional poxin family members.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TLC assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: XCV poxin retains a high degree of specificity for 2′3′-cGAMP, similar to poxins tested from within each other group of enzymes.
source: XCV poxin retains a high degree of specificity for 2′3′-cGAMP, similar to poxins tested from within each other group of enzymes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by specificity assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: XCV and SLV2 poxins are active proteases that self-cleave during expression and purification.
source: SLV2 and XCV poxin proteins are active proteases. Self-cleavage during expression and purification allows separation of a SUMO-poxin fragment from a C-terminal GFP tag.
evidence: This is demonstrated by protein purification and gel analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mutation to the amarillovirus poxin predicted protease catalytic site disrupts all detectable cleavage.
source: Mutation to the amarillovirus poxin predicted protease catalytic site disrupts all detectable cleavage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Edman degradation mapping identifies a conserved cleavage site in the C-terminus of SLV2 poxin and XCV poxin demonstrating strict recognition of an H/ST motif.
source: Using Edman degradation, we mapped the XCV and SLV2 cleavage motifs to an identical H/ST sequence conserved in both viruses (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Edman degradation analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Removal of the mapped cleavage site from the XCV poxin–GFP fusion construct abrogates all detectable proteolysis.
source: Removal of the mapped cleavage site from the XCV poxin–GFP fusion construct abrogates all detectable proteolysis, confirming this motif is required for self-cleavage (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by deletion mutagenesis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The histidine residue at position P1 directly N-terminal to the scissile bond is critical for cleavage site recognition in XCV poxin.
source: Further, mutation of individual residues in the XCV poxin cleavage site motif demonstrates that the histidine residue at position P1 directly N-terminal to the scissile bond is critical for cleavage site recognition (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by alanine scanning mutagenesis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The cleavage site motif NxQH occurs in only two instances across the entire 7070 amino-acid XCV polyprotein.
source: A search of the XCV polyprotein for the cleavage site motif NxQH (Figure 5F) reveals that this motif occurs in only two instances across the entire 7070 amino-acid polyprotein, at the mapped C-terminal cleavage site and again just N-terminal to the poxin-like region (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: XCV poxin may be adapted for self-excision at both the N- and C-termini.
source: Conservation of this motif at only these two positions in the polyprotein suggests that XCV poxin may be adapted for self-excision at both the N- and C-termini (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of cleavage motifs at both termini.

claim: The ability of XCV poxin to catalyze both auto-proteolysis and nucleolytic cleavage of 2′3′-cGAMP confirms the existence of functional self-cleaving poxin enzymes within insect (+)ssRNA viruses.
source: Notably, the ability of XCV poxin to catalyze both auto-proteolysis and nucleolytic cleavage of 2′3′-cGAMP (Figure 5C,E) confirms the existence of functional self-cleaving poxin enzymes within insect (+)ssRNA viruses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by combined nuclease and protease activity assays shown in Figure 5C,E.

claim: Poxins are a widespread family of enzymes dedicated to 2′3′-cGAMP degradation and control of cGAS-STING immunity.
source: Our results reveal that poxins are a widespread family of enzymes dedicated to 2′3′-cGAMP degradation and control of cGAS-STING immunity.
evidence: This is supported by the comprehensive biochemical and phylogenetic analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Acquisition of a C-terminal domain enabled protease dimerization and creation of a new binding site for 2′3′-cGAMP recognition.
source: In this model, acquisition of a C-terminal domain enabled protease dimerization and creation of a new binding site for 2′3′-cGAMP recognition (Figure 6).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis showing the nuclease active site forms at the dimer interface.

claim: Nearly all insect viruses which encode a poxin enzyme exclusively infect moths and butterflies in the order Lepidoptera.
source: Our phylogenetic analysis further emphasizes that nearly all insect viruses which encode a poxin enzyme exclusively infect moths and butterflies in the order Lepidoptera.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and host range information for identified viruses.

claim: Moths and butterflies and their pathogens represent an epicenter for extensive radiation of the poxin protein family.
source: As lepidopteran hosts also encode endogenized versions of poxin, our results reveal moths and butterflies and their pathogens as an epicenter for extensive radiation of this protein family.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution showing greatest diversity in Lepidoptera and their viruses.

claim: The most divergent poxin enzyme sequences are encoded in the genomes of (+)ssRNA viruses from the order Amarillovirales.
source: The most divergent poxin enzyme sequences are encoded in the genomes of (+)ssRNA viruses from the order Amarillovirales, distantly related to mammalian (+)ssRNA pathogens like dengue virus and hepatitis C virus.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Horizontal transfer from an ancient amarillovirus likely seeded poxin diversification in Lepidoptera and eventual acquisition by mammalian poxviruses.
source: Horizontal transfer from an ancient amarillovirus likely seeded poxin diversification in Lepidoptera and eventual acquisition by mammalian poxviruses.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis showing amarilloviruses as the most divergent group.

claim: Amarillovirus genomes encoding poxin have been identified in geographically distant locations and from extremely diverse insect species representing six different phylogenetic orders.
source: Amarillovirus genomes encoding poxin have been identified in geographically distant locations and from extremely diverse insect species representing six different phylogenetic orders (Faizah et al., 2020; Kobayashi et al., 2013; Kondo et al., 2020; Remnant et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2016; Teixeira et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous virus discovery studies.

claim: In mammals, poxin functions to degrade 2′3′-cGAMP and block induction of antiviral signaling by the cGAS-STING pathway during poxvirus infection.
source: In mammals, poxin functions to degrade 2′3′-cGAMP and block induction of antiviral signaling by the cGAS-STING pathway during poxvirus infection (Eaglesham et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In most mammalian poxviruses, poxin exists as a fusion to a C-terminal domain with homology to mammalian schlafens.
source: In most mammalian poxviruses, poxin exists as a fusion to a C-terminal domain with homology to mammalian schlafens (Eaglesham et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The schlafen domain is dispensable for evasion of cGAS-STING signaling in ectromelia virus.
source: Recent work with ectromelia virus demonstrates the schlafen domain is dispensable for evasion of cGAS-STING signaling, and that mammalian schlafens fail to complement poxin–schlafen deletion mutant viruses (Hernáez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: The widespread distribution of poxin enzymes in insect viruses supports a prominent role for 2′3′-cGAMP-signaling in metazoan antiviral immunity.
source: The widespread distribution of poxin enzymes in insect viruses supports a prominent role for 2′3′-cGAMP-signaling in metazoan antiviral immunity.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution and biochemical activity of poxins.

claim: Drosophila STING drives NF-κB and autophagy signaling to restrict viral infection.
source: Recent studies of cGAS-STING signaling in insects have demonstrated that Drosophila STING drives NF-κB and autophagy signaling to restrict viral infection (Goto et al., 2018; Gui et al., 2019; Hua et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018b; Martin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The upstream signaling machinery that activates STING in insects remains poorly understood.
source: However, the upstream signaling machinery that activates STING in insects remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Insects encode enzymes like Drosophila melanogaster CG7194 and CG12970 that are part of the cGAS/DncV-like nucleotidyltransferase (CD-NTase) family.
source: Insects encode enzymes like Drosophila melanogaster CG7194 and CG12970 that are part of the cGAS/DncV-like nucleotidyltransferase (CD-NTase) family (Kranzusch, 2019; Whiteley et al., 2019), but these enzymes are significantly divergent from mammalian cGAS and it is unclear if insect CD-NTases synthesize 2′3′-cGAMP or respond to cytosolic DNA.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Nearly all poxin representatives from across all groups retain specificity for 2′3′-cGAMP and fail to cleave 3′3′-cGAMP.
source: Our results show that nearly all poxin representatives from across all groups retain specificity for 2′3′-cGAMP and fail to cleave 3′3′-cGAMP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by specificity assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 2′3′-cGAMP is a predominant ligand in insect immune signaling.
source: Although exceptions to poxin specificity exist (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), these results suggest that 2′3′-cGAMP is a predominant ligand in insect immune signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity of poxins for 2′3′-cGAMP.

claim: Two different parasitoid wasp species encode poxin homologs.
source: Two different parasitoid wasp species encode poxin homologs (Glypta fumiferanae: AKD28026 and Microplitis demolitor: XP_008552911), and previous work suggests these proteins may even play a role in parasitism of caterpillars, within which the wasps lay their eggs (Béliveau et al., 2015; Burke et al., 2018; Strand and Burke, 2015).
evidence: This is based on sequence identification and supported by citations.

claim: The mayfly Ephemera danica encodes a poxin homolog which possesses an intact HYK catalytic triad indicating functional poxin nuclease activity.
source: Further, the mayfly Ephemera danica encodes a poxin homolog (KAF4524375), which possesses an intact HYK catalytic triad indicating functional poxin nuclease activity, but this enzyme fails to cluster within other poxin groups (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and phylogenetic placement shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Insect poxins may function to limit the magnitude of STING activation.
source: One hypothesis is that insect poxins function to limit the magnitude of STING activation.
evidence: This is proposed as a hypothesis based on kinetic differences.

claim: Viral poxins are capable of degrading 2′3′-cGAMP even at low ligand concentrations, while host poxins appear tailored for setting an upper threshold for the immune response.
source: Although viral poxins are capable of degrading 2′3′-cGAMP even at low ligand concentrations, host poxins instead appear tailored for setting an upper threshold for the immune response.
evidence: This is inferred from kinetic differences shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In mammals, 2′3′-cGAMP can be released from infected cells and imported to activate bystander immunity.
source: In mammals, a growing body of work suggests that 2′3′-cGAMP can be released from infected cells and imported to activate bystander immunity (Carozza et al., 2020; Luteijn et al., 2019; Ritchie et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Many baculoviruses encode two different poxin enzymes with one variant containing a signal peptide for extracellular secretion.
source: Interestingly, our bioinformatic analysis demonstrates that many baculoviruses encode two different poxin enzymes with one variant containing a signal peptide for extracellular secretion (Figure 6A; Craveiro et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 6A and supported by citation.

claim: Host lepidopteran poxins are encoded as multiple isoforms with and without signal peptides.
source: Likewise, host lepidopteran poxins are encoded as multiple isoforms with and without a signal peptides (e.g. Trichoplusia ni XP_026730193 and XP_026730202) (Supplementary file 1; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and supported by citation.

claim: In insects, poxins may regulate extracellular 2′3′-cGAMP signaling in addition to controlling cytosolic cGAS-STING activation.
source: In insects, poxins may therefore regulate extracellular 2′3′-cGAMP signaling in addition to controlling cytosolic cGAS-STING activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of signal peptides in some poxin isoforms.

claim: The only enzyme known to degrade 2′3′-cGAMP in humans is the nuclease ENPP1, which is exclusively extracellular.
source: In contrast to the widespread distribution of poxin enzymes among insects and insect viruses, there is a puzzling lack of cytosolic 2′3′-cGAMP nuclease machinery in mammalian cells (Eaglesham et al., 2019). The only enzyme known to degrade 2′3′-cGAMP in humans is the nuclease ENPP1, which is exclusively extracellular and regulates signaling outside of the cell (Carozza et al., 2020; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Functional homologs of ENPP1 have not been identified in insects.
source: Functional homologs of ENPP1 have not been identified in insects, indicating that alternative mechanisms for regulating cGAS-STING signaling may exist in these animals.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap and used to support the hypothesis about poxin function.

claim: This abundance of enzymes that efficiently degrade 2′3′-cGAMP in the cytosol of insects may have provided the opportunity for poxviruses to acquire a new mechanism of immune control that did not exist in mammalian cells.
source: This abundance of enzymes that efficiently degrade 2′3′-cGAMP in the cytosol of insects may have provided the opportunity for poxviruses to acquire a new mechanism of immune control that did not exist in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution and functional differences between insect and mammalian systems.

claim: Poxins have traversed a vast evolutionary distance from an origin in insect (+)ssRNA viruses to a role in enabling mammalian poxvirus pathogens to evade cGAS-STING immunity.
source: Poxins have traversed a vast evolutionary distance from an origin in insect (+)ssRNA viruses to a role in enabling mammalian poxvirus pathogens to evade cGAS-STING immunity, and a remarkable transition from protease to nuclease activity provides a clear example of how proteins can evolve through gain and loss of enzymatic function.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by all the phylogenetic and biochemical data presented.

claim: Acquisition of poxins from insect viruses underscores the functional similarities between mammalian and insect innate immunity.
source: Acquisition of poxins from insect viruses further underscores the functional similarities between mammalian and insect innate immunity and reveals the importance of environmental genetic diversity as a driver for evolution of pathogenic viruses.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful horizontal transfer and functional conservation of poxins.
